The captured variables can still be accessed outside of the original function's execution context, even if the function itself has already completed.
This ability to access variables from an earlier part of the codebase allows closures to provide encapsulation and maintain state across multiple function calls. It also enables features like memoization and lazy evaluation, where functions can remember previous results and reuse them without recalculating them every time they're called.
While this behavior may seem similar to how variables would behave if they weren't present in the local scope, the key difference lies in the fact that closures capture the entire environment in which the function was defined, rather than simply accessing variables that happen to exist at the same level of the call stack. This means that closures have more flexibility and power compared to simple variable hoisting or shadowing.
